title: Matthew 3:1–6
context: Years after the Nazareth settlement, Matthew jumps to John’s public ministry: a wilderness preacher calls Israel to repent because the kingdom of heaven is near, fulfills Isaiah’s voice, and baptizes confessing crowds in the Jordan.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: How earlier teachers on both sides handled years after the Nazareth settlement, quoted directly.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: In those days - that is, while Jesus dwelt there. In the wilderness of Judea - This was a wilderness properly so called, a wild, barren, desolate place as was that also where our Lord was tempted. But, generally speaking, a wilderness in the New Testament means only a common, or less cultivated place, in opposition to pasture and arable land.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 3:1–6)

reformed.quote: Repent ye Matthew differs from the other two Evangelists in this respect, that he relates the substance of John's doctrine, as uttered by John himself, while they relate it in their own words; though Mark has one word more than Luke: for he says, he came Baptizing, and preaching the baptism of repentance But in substance there is the most perfect agreement: for they all connect repentance with the forgiveness of sins. The kingdom of God among men is nothing else than a restoration to a happy life; or, in other words, it is true and everlasting happiness.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 3:1–6)

verses.text: In those days, John the Baptizer came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
Matthew opens the adult story with a preacher, not a palace. John appears in the wilderness of Judea with a word for the nation.

Arminians often stress that God sends a sincere call through human heralds. The wilderness setting strips away religious comfort so the message can be heard. God prepares the way before the King arrives.
verses.reformedNotes:
“In those days” is providence, not accident. The Baptist arrives on schedule in the place God chose for a preparatory ministry.

John’s appearing is God’s initiative. The wilderness preacher is a gift to Israel before the Son’s public work begins.

verses.text: “Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!”
verses.arminianNotes:
The first word is repent, and the reason is nearness of the kingdom. Turn because the King is near, not merely because life is hard.

The call is serious and for the hearers. Grace awakens; people remain responsible to turn. Both traditions preach that kingdom nearness demands a changed mind and life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Repentance is required because God’s reign has drawn near. The kingdom does not wait on human scheduling.

God brings His kingdom; the call to repent is His sovereign summons. Where the Word runs, hearts are confronted with the King who is already advancing.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat repentance as urgent under a near kingdom. Arminians typically underline a sincere, grace-enabled call all hearers should answer; Calvinists stress God’s initiative in bringing the kingdom and effectually summoning His people to turn.

verses.text: For this is he who was spoken of by Isaiah the prophet, saying, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness, make the way of the Lord ready! Make his paths straight!”
verses.arminianNotes:
John is not inventing a brand; he is Isaiah’s voice. Preparation means clearing obstacles so the Lord may come.

God has long intended this invitation. Prophecy becomes preaching so people can prepare. Straight paths are something hearers are called to make under grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew ties John to written prophecy. The Lord has a way, and He sends a voice to announce it.

Scripture’s promise lands in history. The wilderness cry is God’s own plan unfolding so that the Lord Himself will walk among His people.

verses.text: Now John himself wore clothing made of camel’s hair with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey.
verses.arminianNotes:
Camel’s hair, leather belt, locusts, and wild honey mark John as a prophet in Elijah’s line, not a court chaplain. His life matches his message of urgency.

Pastoral shared note: authenticity matters. A call to repent loses force when the messenger’s life is padded with the comforts he will not challenge.
verses.reformedNotes:
John’s austere dress and diet signal prophetic continuity. God equips His herald with a life that fits the word.

Even the messenger’s habits sit under providence. The focus remains the Word he carries, not a cult of personality.

verses.text: Then people from Jerusalem, all of Judea, and all the region around the Jordan went out to him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Crowds stream from city and countryside. The Word draws people out of ordinary routines toward repentance and baptism.

When the gospel is preached with clarity, many may come. Drawing is gracious and wide in the narrative’s first movement—yet coming still requires response.
verses.reformedNotes:
A regional movement gathers at the Jordan. God is stirring Israel before the Messiah’s public debut.

Such going-out is not random revivalism alone; it is the Lord preparing a people by His Word through His prophet.

verses.text: They were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.
verses.arminianNotes:
Baptism joins confession. Immersion in the Jordan is not empty ritual; sins are named and turned from.

Classical Arminians press honesty here: grace invites confession, and people truly confess. Shared confession across traditions: forgiveness is sought by admitting guilt, not by hiding behind pedigree.
verses.reformedNotes:
Confession and baptism mark those who answer John’s call. Sin is acknowledged under the Word.

True repentance includes open confession. God grants a people who tell the truth about themselves as they await the mightier One still to come.
verses.keyContrast: Both honor baptism with confession as turning. Arminians often emphasize sincere, grace-enabled response; Reformed readers often emphasize God’s preparatory work producing a confessing people under His Word.
